prompt: A lesson quotes 0.01040 dollars an hour for a `t3.micro`. Which region is that, and what is left out of the price?
hint: Two columns, and one line of the header about money.

choices.text: `sa-east-1`, before tax
choices.why: São Paulo's line for that machine is 0.01680. The Brazilian region is the dearer column on every line of the sheet.

choices.text: `us-east-1`, before tax
choices.why: Right. The second column is Northern Virginia, and the header says every price excludes tax.

choices.text: `us-east-1`, with tax already included in it
choices.why: The header says the opposite: USD, excluding tax. A real bill adds it on top.

choices.text: Whichever region the program was run from
choices.why: The sheet has two fixed columns read from published files. Where the laptop sits changes nothing.

prompt: Why does `prices.py` print the same prices next year as it does today?
hint: Look at the word after each offer's name.

choices.text: It reads pinned versions of each offer
choices.why: Right. A published version does not change: keep the versions and you get the same sheet, change them and you get newer prices.

choices.text: AWS never changes a published price within a year
choices.why: Prices move all the time, which is exactly why the program pins something.

choices.text: The prices were typed into the program by hand
choices.why: Nothing is typed: it reads AWS's own JSON files and prints what they say.

choices.text: It reads only its local cache, which nobody updates
choices.why: The cache saves a download. Empty it and the program fetches the same pinned versions again.

prompt: At the sheet's prices, how many dollars an hour more does a `t3.micro` cost in `sa-east-1` than in `us-east-1`?
What else does *it's just somebody else's computer* describe as well as it describes the cloud?
hint: Renting a computer is older than the web.

choices.text: A server in your own office
choices.why: That is your own computer; the sentence at least rules it out.

choices.text: Nothing else: it is the definition of the cloud
choices.why: It fits colocation and dedicated hosting just as well, so it cannot define anything.

choices.text: A virtual machine, but never a finished application
choices.why: A finished application runs on somebody else's computer too. The sentence does not separate the models at all.

choices.text: A server rented from a 1990s hosting company
choices.why: Right, and that is why the sentence is true and useless: it leaves out what changed.

prompt: Which differences between older hosting and the cloud does the sentence leave out? Choose all that apply.
hint: The sentence is only about whose computer it is.

choices.text: You get the machine by asking an API, with no person involved
choices.why: Right. How you get it is the first thing that changed.

choices.text: The machine sits in a building the provider owns
choices.why: True of both, and it is the one part the sentence does capture.

choices.text: You pay by the unit you used
choices.why: Right. Hours, gigabytes or requests, instead of a flat month.

choices.text: You can hand it back tomorrow and stop paying
choices.why: Right. With a yearly contract you pay for January whether you need the machine or not.

prompt: A machine costs 0.01680 dollars an hour. Taking a month as 730 hours, what does it cost for one month?
hint: Hours times the price per hour.

prompt: Match each instance to the NIST characteristic it shows.
hint: One characteristic per instance.

pairs.left: A request at 3 a.m. creates a machine and nobody at the provider reads it
The same account is managed from a laptop, a phone or a script
A `t3.micro` is a slice of a far larger server
Two machines most of the year, ten in the week of a sale
Storage is billed by the gigabyte-month

prompt: A company rents you a physical server by the month. You order it with a form and a technician installs it. Which of the five characteristics does it have?
hint: The lesson's table found one.

choices.text: Resource pooling
choices.why: The whole machine is yours, and sits idle when you do.

choices.text: Broad network access
choices.why: Right. You reach it over the internet like anything else, and that is all it shares with the cloud.

choices.text: Measured service
choices.why: The price is flat whatever you used, which is the opposite of metering.

choices.text: On-demand self-service
choices.why: A technician installs it. Self-service means no person in the loop.

prompt: A provider creates machines through an API, bills them by the hour and runs them on shared hardware. Every new machine waits for an employee to approve it, which takes a working day. Which characteristic is missing?
hint: Who takes part in answering the request?

choices.text: Measured service
choices.why: Billing by the hour is metering, and this provider has it.

choices.text: Resource pooling
choices.why: Shared hardware is pooling, and this provider has it.

choices.text: None: an API is all it takes to be cloud
choices.why: The API is only the door. The person behind it is what the first characteristic rules out.

choices.text: On-demand self-service
choices.why: Right. However good the API, an approval by a person is exactly what self-service excludes.

prompt: NIST calls the property of being billed by the hour, the gigabyte or the request ___ service.
hint: What the meter does.

prompt: Why can a shop get ten machines in the week of a sale without having ordered them months before?
hint: Where do the ten come from?

choices.text: Because the provider bills by the hour
choices.why: Metering is how you pay for them. It is not where they come from.

choices.text: The API reserved them for the shop in advance
choices.why: Nothing was reserved. The shop asked that week and got them that week.

choices.text: Spare capacity that all its customers share
choices.why: Right. Elasticity is what pooling buys: the spare room belongs to everybody at once.

choices.text: The shop's own servers were moved into the provider's building
choices.why: Moving servers is older hosting. The ten machines were never the shop's.

prompt: Put these layers in order, from the bottom of the stack to the top.
hint: Start with what you can touch.
trap: Runtime below the operating system is the usual slip: the interpreter is a program the operating system runs.

prompt: Which layer cannot be bought or downloaded again once it is lost?
hint: Everything else is a purchase or a download.

choices.text: The application
choices.why: The code lives in a repository and can be deployed again.

choices.text: The operating system
choices.why: An operating system is an image you download again in minutes.

choices.text: The hardware
choices.why: Hardware is a purchase. Expensive, but it can be made again.

choices.text: The data
choices.why: Right. Last month's orders exist only where you put them.

prompt: Match each job to the layer it belongs to.
hint: Ask what the job touches.

pairs.left: Moving off a Python version whose support is ending
Closing the database port to the internet
Removing the login of somebody who left

prompt: On IaaS, who installs the security updates for the virtual machine's operating system?
hint: Where is the line?

choices.text: You, or a setting you switched on
choices.why: Right. Even automatic updates are your setting, on your side of the line.

choices.text: The provider, as part of the price
choices.why: The provider stops at the virtualisation layer and never logs in to your machine.

choices.text: The provider, but only on the images it supplies
choices.why: Supplying the image is not updating the machine that started from it.

choices.text: Nobody: images come patched when you create them
choices.why: An image is patched up to the day it was built. From then on the machine ages.

prompt: At the sheet's São Paulo price for a `gp3` volume, what does a 50 GB disk cost per month?
hint: 0.1520 per GB-month.

prompt: The web server on your virtual machine crashed at four in the morning, and the provider's dashboard still shows the machine as healthy. Why?
hint: What does the provider watch?

choices.text: The dashboard is refreshed only once a day
choices.why: Refreshing it would change nothing: the machine really is healthy.

choices.text: Its checks cover the layers below the line, and the crash is above it
choices.why: Right. Hardware and hypervisor are fine; a program you run is not the provider's to watch.

choices.text: A crashed web server stops the whole machine, so the dashboard is wrong
choices.why: The machine keeps running without its web server, which is why nothing looks wrong.

choices.text: Health checks are switched off on the smallest machines
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it. No check of the provider's reaches your web server.

prompt: Rebuilding the servers a company already had as virtual machines, with as little change as possible, is called lift and ___.
hint: Two short verbs that rhyme.

prompt: A shop on a PaaS saves uploaded product photos to its own local disk, and they vanish after the next deploy. What went wrong?
hint: What happens to a copy of the application when it is replaced?

choices.text: Local files go when a copy is replaced
choices.why: Right. Files that must survive belong in object storage, which lesson 5 describes.

choices.text: The platform deletes every file older than a day
choices.why: Age has nothing to do with it. A photo saved a minute before the deploy is lost too.

choices.text: The photos went over the platform's memory limit
choices.why: Memory is where a program works, not where a file is stored.

choices.text: The deploy ran as another user, who cannot see them
choices.why: The photos are gone, not hidden. The copy that held them no longer exists.

prompt: On PaaS, a security hole is announced in the web framework your code lists among its packages. Whose job is the fix?
hint: Is the framework the runtime, or something the application imports?

choices.text: The platform's, because it patches the runtime
choices.why: It patches the interpreter. The framework is a package of the application, above the line.

choices.text: The framework's authors, who push it into running applications
choices.why: They publish a fixed version. Nobody installs it in your shop but you.

choices.text: Yours: update the version, test and deploy
choices.why: Right. Everything the application imports sits on your side of the line, exactly as on IaaS.

choices.text: Nobody's, until the platform retires that version
choices.why: Retiring a runtime version is a different event, and the hole stays open until then.

prompt: Which of these do you give up when an application moves from a virtual machine to a PaaS? Choose all that apply.
hint: What did the platform take off your side of the line?

choices.text: Deciding which packages your code imports
choices.why: That is the application row, still yours on PaaS.

choices.text: Installing any system package you like
choices.why: Right. There is no machine of yours to install it on.

choices.text: Controlling who may deploy to the platform account
choices.why: Access is identity, the top row, yours in every model.

choices.text: A runtime version outside the platform's list
choices.why: Right. The platform's menu is your menu.

prompt: A folder of contracts kept in a document service turns up in a search engine. The provider had no breach. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Which row of the stack decides who sees a folder?

choices.text: The provider's encryption failed
choices.why: Encryption protects the disks. The folder was served to anyone who asked, as its setting allowed.

choices.text: Anybody can read what is on SaaS by default
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so. Somebody chose this folder's setting.

choices.text: It was shared as *anyone with the link can view*
choices.why: Right. The provider's security was flawless and the folder public anyway, because a setting said so.

choices.text: The search engine bought access from the provider
choices.why: No provider sells that; the folder was simply open.

prompt: Which of these is still your job on SaaS?
hint: Two rows are left above the line.

choices.text: Choosing the application's version
choices.why: The application changes when the provider changes it, for everybody at once.

choices.text: Restarting the application when it crashes
choices.why: The application is below the line on SaaS. You would not even see it crash.

choices.text: Patching the servers it runs on
choices.why: Every layer up to the application is the provider's on SaaS.

choices.text: Removing a leaver's account
choices.why: Right. Only you know who works for you.

prompt: An employee deletes a year of customer records from a SaaS CRM, and nobody notices for four months. What decides whether they come back?
hint: The provider's copies protect against whose failures?

choices.text: The provider's window for keeping deleted items
choices.why: Right. Past that window they are gone for good, whatever the provider's own copies do.

choices.text: Nothing: the provider keeps every version of everything
choices.why: Deleted items are kept for a limited window in many services, not forever.

choices.text: The provider's copies against disk failure, which cover this
choices.why: Those copies protect against the provider's failures. They faithfully copy your deletion too.

choices.text: Whether the employee still has a working login
choices.why: Their login decides who could delete more, not whether the records return.

prompt: Before relying on a SaaS product, find out what its ___ gives you, while leaving is still a choice rather than an emergency.
hint: The button that hands you your own records as a file.

prompt: Counting the ten rows of the lesson's drawing, how many are yours on PaaS?
hint: Everything above the runtime.

prompt: AWS sums up the shared responsibility model in two phrases. Which one is the customer's half?
hint: One preposition puts you inside.

choices.text: Security *of* the cloud
choices.why: That is AWS's half: the buildings, the hardware, the hypervisor.

choices.text: Security *in* the cloud
choices.why: Right. What you put in the cloud and how you set it up is yours.

choices.text: Security *for* the cloud
choices.why: Not one of the model's two phrases.

choices.text: Security *by* the cloud
choices.why: Not one of the two phrases either; it would hand the whole job to AWS.

prompt: A company has its email on SaaS, its website on a platform and an accounting program on a virtual machine. The director asks: are we patched? What is the useful answer?
hint: How many lines does this company have?

choices.text: Three answers, one for each system and its line
choices.why: Right: nothing for the email, the site's packages, and the whole accounting machine. One line per system, at three heights.

choices.text: Yes, all three are in the cloud
choices.why: Being in the cloud says nothing about which rows are yours.

choices.text: Only the accounting machine needs checking
choices.why: The website's packages sit above the PaaS line, so they are yours too.

choices.text: It depends on which provider has the weakest security
choices.why: The question is about the rows on your side, and no provider patches those.

prompt: Order these from the one that leaves you the most rows to the one that leaves you the fewest.
hint: The line goes up at each step.
items: A server in your own room
A platform you push code to
trap: Putting the platform before the virtual machine is the slip: a platform takes the operating system and the runtime as well.

prompt: On a service that runs your container image, the language runtime packaged inside the image gets a security fix. Whose job is it?
hint: Where does the runtime live now?

choices.text: The provider's, as on PaaS
choices.why: On PaaS the platform installs the runtime. Here you packaged it yourself.

choices.text: The provider's, because it patches the host
choices.why: It patches the host's operating system. The runtime travels inside your image.

choices.text: Nobody's: a container is isolated, so no fix is needed
choices.why: Isolation limits what a hole reaches. It does not close the hole.

choices.text: Yours: rebuild the image with the fix, then deploy it
choices.why: Right. CaaS puts the line below the runtime, so the runtime's patches come back to you.

prompt: Match each kind of service to what you hand over to it.
hint: The name says what you hand over.

pairs.right: One function that answers one event
A choice of machine image, then everything above it
Nothing but your data and your users

prompt: On a managed database the engine and its patches are the provider's; the queries, the indexes, the users and the ___ stay yours.
hint: What you designed the tables as, or what is in them.

prompt: Barro is on IaaS, and nobody there installs Tuesday's fix for the TLS library. What happens?
hint: Who else would log in to the machine?

choices.text: The provider installs it after a grace period
choices.why: The provider never logs in to a customer's machine, grace period or not.

choices.text: The shop stops serving HTTPS until the fix is in
choices.why: Nothing stops it. The old library keeps working, hole included.

choices.text: Nothing visible: the shop keeps selling on the vulnerable library
choices.why: Right. The failure has no symptom, which is why it lasts until somebody notices.

choices.text: The operating system refuses to start the web server
choices.why: An operating system does not refuse an old library; it loads what is installed.

prompt: Barro's PaaS builds operating-system fixes into the application only when it is next deployed. Nobody has deployed for a month. What is the state of the shop?
hint: When does the fix reach the running shop on this kind of platform?

choices.text: Patched, since the platform owns the operating system
choices.why: It owns it, and on this platform the fix only arrives with a deploy.

choices.text: Stopped by the platform until somebody deploys
choices.why: The platform keeps the old copy running. Nothing stops.

choices.text: Patched in the library, but its web framework is out of date
choices.why: The framework is a separate question. Here the operating system's library itself is old.

choices.text: Running last month's library until the next deploy
choices.why: Right. Knowing which kind of platform you are on is your part of the job.

prompt: Barro is on IaaS. Put its response to Tuesday's TLS fix in order.
hint: The last step is the one from the customer's side.
items: Restart every program that loaded the old library
Check that the shop still answers
trap: Skipping the restart is the usual slip: a program that loaded the old library keeps using it until it starts again.

prompt: Which of Barro's jobs is the same on IaaS, on PaaS and on SaaS?
hint: Look for a row that never moves.

choices.text: Updating the web framework
choices.why: On SaaS there is no Barro code, so it is the provider's there.

choices.text: Removing the access of somebody who leaves
choices.why: Right. Identity is above the line in every model.

choices.text: Installing the fix for the TLS library
choices.why: Only on IaaS is it Barro's; above that it crosses the line.

choices.text: Restarting the web server
choices.why: On PaaS and SaaS there is no web server of Barro's to restart.

prompt: A program needs a kernel setting and a system package that no platform installs. Which model does that point to?
hint: Which row does it need to hold?

choices.text: PaaS
choices.why: The platform holds the operating system row, which is the one this program needs.

choices.text: SaaS
choices.why: SaaS runs somebody else's program, not yours.

choices.text: IaaS
choices.why: Right. Only on IaaS is the operating system yours to configure.

choices.text: FaaS
choices.why: Functions sit even higher than a platform, further from the kernel.

prompt: A company must keep its customers' data in Brazil. What does that requirement decide?
hint: Two separate choices: who runs the rows, and where they run.

choices.text: IaaS, because only machines have a location
choices.why: Every model runs somewhere. A platform in São Paulo keeps data in Brazil as well.

choices.text: The region, and nothing about the model
choices.why: Right. Who runs the rows and where they run are chosen separately.

choices.text: A server in the company's own building
choices.why: A region inside the country does it without a building of your own.

choices.text: PaaS, because a managed service is local
choices.why: Managed says who does the work, not where it is done.

prompt: Which statement about lock-in matches the lesson?
hint: Is it a defect or a price?

choices.text: It is a defect to avoid at any cost
choices.why: A managed service can save more work than a move would ever cost.

choices.text: It only exists on SaaS
choices.why: A platform's build files and add-ons tie you too, and so does any managed service.

choices.text: It disappears when the provider is large enough
choices.why: Size changes nothing about what you would have to redo to leave.

choices.text: It is a price, cheapest to learn before you choose
choices.why: Right. Its cost is decided on the day you pick the model.

prompt: A school uses a hosted learning platform, sold as SaaS. A parent asks who can see their child's grades. Who has to answer?
hint: Which rows are left above the line on SaaS?

choices.text: The school: who has access is its row on every model
choices.why: Right. The provider built the permissions; the school chose who gets them.

choices.text: The provider, which runs the application
choices.why: Running the application does not tell it which teachers should see which class.

choices.text: Nobody: on SaaS the data belongs to the provider
choices.why: The data is yours on every model. The provider only stores it.

choices.text: The provider, since it wrote the permission system
choices.why: It wrote the tool. The settings inside it are the school's.

prompt: At the sheet's Lambda price per million requests, what do 3 million requests cost, leaving the free tier out?
hint: 0.20 per million.

prompt: AWS's name for the line between its jobs and the customer's is the shared ___ model.
hint: Who answers for what.

prompt: Match each situation to the model it describes.
hint: Ask what you are touching.

pairs.left: You log in over SSH and run `apt upgrade`
You push code and pick Python from the platform's list
You change a sharing setting on the admin page
You upload one function billed per GB-second
